DOCUMENT:
"""
Purpose: The aim of this study was to develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance. The motivation is to support standardized reporting and improve report quality in clinical practice, thereby enhancing communication, reducing errors, and improving patient care in radiology.

Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 638 radiology reports from CT examinations of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists in 2023 and 2024. The multi-agent AI pipeline consisted of three sequential agents: (1) a structuring agent that segmented reports into standardized anatomical sections at the sentence level using regex rules and local large language models; (2) a consistency-checking agent that detected mismatches between the Findings and Impression sections or within sections; and (3) a QA agent that identified gender-anatomy conflicts and undocumented communication of critical findings using rule-based and language model prompts. Each agent operated independently, passing its output to the next agent in sequence; feedback loops or automated error correction between agents were not implemented in this version to maintain modularity and facilitate error tracing. The system’s structuring and QA functions were evaluated together as a unified workflow. For radiologist evaluation, a random subset of 45 reports was selected using stratified random sampling to represent the distribution of body regions (chest, abdomen, pelvis) and the types of flagged issues (section mismatches, gender-anatomy conflicts, critical findings) present in the full dataset. Two board-certified radiologists independently reviewed these reports. “Correctly restructured” was defined as accurate anatomical section assignment for the entire report without altering original content; “incorrectly restructured” indicated misassignment or loss of information at the report level; “disagreement” reflected differing reviewer assessments per report. In cases of disagreement, no consensus process was used; this approach was chosen to capture independent reviewer perspectives and avoid bias from forced agreement. Inter-rater agreement was calculated using Cohen’s kappa.

Results: The multi-agent system structured the Findings sections of all 638 reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format while retaining the original report content. The system flagged 90 of 638 reports (14.1%, 95% CI: 11.5–17.0%) for at least one issue: section mismatches (80 of 638 reports, 12.5%, 95% CI: 10.1–15.4%), gender-anatomy conflicts (5 of 638 reports, 0.8%), and undocumented communication of critical findings (3 of 638 reports, 0.5%). In the radiologist evaluation, both reviewers agreed that 31 of 45 reports (69%, 95% CI: 53–82%) were correctly restructured, 2 of 45 reports (4%, 95% CI: 0–13%) were incorrectly restructured, and there was disagreement on 12 of 45 reports (27%, 95% CI: 15–42%). Cohen’s kappa for agreement was 0.62, which is generally interpreted as substantial agreement (values between 0.61 and 0.80 are considered substantial; see Landis and Koch, 1977). Both reviewers independently assessed whether any clinically important information was omitted or any fabricated content was introduced, using an open-ended review of each report; both agreed that neither occurred. Overall QA performance was rated as "excellent" in 24 of 45 reports (53%), "good" in 14 of 45 reports (31%), and "fair" in 7 of 45 reports (16%), corresponding to 38 of 45 reports (84%, 95% CI: 70–93%) rated as "excellent" or "good".

Conclusion: A locally deployed multi-agent AI system combined radiology report structuring and quality assurance within a single workflow, demonstrating favorable performance in radiologist evaluation.

Limitations:
- Retrospective design
- Single-institution setting
- Limited sample size for radiologist evaluation
- Potential sources of error such as misclassification of anatomical sections or missed inconsistencies
- Generalizability to other institutions, imaging modalities, or report types remains to be established

Future work will focus on expanding the system to additional report types, incorporating automated feedback mechanisms between agents, and further improving error detection. The study was conducted with institutional review board approval and in compliance with data privacy regulations; all data were anonymized and stored on secure, access-controlled servers. Such systems may support standardization of reporting and quality assurance in radiology practice, with the potential to streamline workflows and improve clinical communication.
"""
